planting.note: Set a single detached joint on its side, barely pressed into sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun, and leave it undisturbed until roots form along the underside.

directions: This is the most cold-tolerant cactus native to North America, ranging farther north into Canada than any other species and surviving winters that dip well below -30 degrees F when kept dry at the roots. Small, egg-shaped, easily detached joints give the plant its common name, since even light contact can snap off segments that root readily wherever they land, forming loose, low mats over gravelly slopes and prairie outcrops. Pale yellow flowers open briefly in late spring atop the previous year's joints. Site it in lean, fast-draining mineral soil with no summer irrigation, since wet feet in winter are far more damaging than cold.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Let a cut stem segment callus for one to two weeks in a dry, shaded spot before setting the base an inch into sharply drained, rocky soil; handle only with tongs or heavy leather gloves.

directions: Native to high desert grasslands and pinyon-juniper slopes of Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, and Colorado, this shrubby cholla forms loose, branching thickets of slender, densely spined stems that die back to a woody framework in hard winters and resprout each spring. Pale yellow-green flowers appear in early summer, followed by spiny yellow fruit that can persist through winter. It thrives in rocky, unamended soil with excellent drainage and needs no irrigation once established, but resents heavy clay or standing winter moisture. Because detached joints root readily and the barbed spines penetrate skin and clothing easily, site it away from paths and handle debris with long-handled tongs.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Callus a cut stem segment for one to two weeks, then set the base an inch into sharply drained, sandy or caliche soil in full sun; established plants also self-propagate from fallen joints.

directions: Native from Texas and southern New Mexico into northern Mexico, this open, airy cholla has unusually slender, pencil-thin stems compared to most tree chollas, giving mature plants a wispy, wand-like silhouette. Small magenta-pink flowers appear in late spring, and the bright red, spineless fruit that follows persists on the plant through winter, giving rise to the common name. It tolerates poor, caliche, or rocky soils and extended drought without complaint, needing only sharp drainage and full sun to thrive as a specimen or wildlife-supporting hedge. Winter wet is its main threat, so avoid low spots where water collects after rain.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or a divided clump segment in spring into sharply drained, gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; established mounds are best increased by separating rooted offsets rather than seed.

directions: Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of West Texas, southern New Mexico, and northern Mexico, this hedgehog cactus forms dense, sprawling mounds that can eventually reach several hundred cylindrical stems, each armed with dense straw-colored spines that give the species its epithet. In late spring the mound erupts with large, brilliantly magenta flowers that open for several days, followed by sweet, spineless, strawberry-flavored fruit prized by wildlife and foragers alike. It demands lean, sharply drained, mineral soil and full desert sun, and rots quickly if planted in heavy or poorly drained ground. Established clumps tolerate hard freezes when kept dry but should be shielded from prolonged winter rain in wetter climates.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
